DigiLocker is safer than a plastic folder — unless you download the fake app

On 29 November 2025, the official Digital India handle posted a warning that should have been louder than it was. Fraudulent apps with names like DigiLocker were circulating on app stores. The instruction was blunt: use only the authentic DigiLocker application. If you had already installed a suspicious version, delete it and change the passwords on linked accounts.

Moneycontrol reported the advisory the next day. Times of India followed for students. This is the incident. I am not going to invent a victim. The government warning is the case.

Why a plastic folder loses

A plastic folder can be stolen, soaked, or left on a bus. DigiLocker is safer than that folder for a simple reason. It is not a photo album of papers you scanned. It is a wallet that government issuers can push documents into.

The official site is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. From there you can access, share, and get government-issued documents verified: a driving licence, a vehicle RC, marksheets, and other records the issuer has actually placed in your account.

How it works, without the brochure language

You open an account that is authenticated with Aadhaar. Then an RTO, a school board, a university, or another issuer sends a digitally signed document into that account. When a verifier checks it, they are not squinting at a JPEG you uploaded. They are looking at the issuer's signature.

That is why a screenshot is not the same thing. A screenshot is a picture. An issued DigiLocker document is a signed record from the source. You can crop a marksheet photo in two minutes. You cannot forge the issuer's signature by taking a better photo.

MeitY has been clear on the legal point. Issued documents in DigiLocker are deemed at par with originals. The official about page says the same thing under the IT Act, and in more formal language under Rule 9A of the 2016 Digital Locker rules. You can show a digital driving licence, or pull a Class X or Class XII marksheet, without laminating another photocopy.

That legal status is useful only if you are inside the real locker.

The live warning

A clone that looks like DigiLocker does not need to "hack the government." It only needs you to type an Aadhaar number and share an OTP. DigiLocker does not make you unhackable. The risk moved. Paper used to get lost. Now someone tries to phish the OTP that opens the locker.

The authentic app is published by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Government of India. The official website is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. Install from there, or from the store listing that site points to. Confirm the developer name before you tap Install.

Do not install from a forwarded WhatsApp link. Do not trust a search ad that says "DigiLocker KYC" and asks for an OTP on a random page. No genuine officer needs that code from you on a link they just sent.

If a suspicious version is already on the phone, do what the advisory said. Delete it. Change the passwords on linked accounts. Then install the real app and check which documents are actually sitting there.

What to do before you need it

Before a road trip, open the real app and pull your driving licence and RC. Do it at home, on your own Wi-Fi, while you are not being rushed by a checkpoint or a rental desk.

Before admissions or a job file, students can pull marksheets from the board instead of hunting a laminated copy. If a verifier will accept DigiLocker, give them the issued document, not a crop of your screen.

Never share an OTP for "DigiLocker KYC" on a random link. The locker is tied to Aadhaar. The OTP is the key. Anyone who wants the key on a page you did not open from https://t.co/AE2sh860xw is not helping you file a document.

If you already downloaded something that only looked official, treat it as a live problem, not an embarrassing mistake. Delete the app. Change passwords. Watch bank and Aadhaar-linked SMS for a few days. Then start again from the official site.

The honest limit

A plastic folder fails when you lose it. DigiLocker fails when you hand the key to a lookalike. The folder is still worse for rain. The lookalike is worse for everything else.

Use the real locker. Pull the issued document, not a screenshot. Keep the OTP to yourself. That is the whole guide.

This article is written for general education and is not legal advice. It does not claim DigiLocker cannot be abused. The risk moved from lost paper to phishing for your Aadhaar OTP.

Sources: DigiLocker official site https://t.co/T2NXjM8lAm; DigiLocker About (issued documents at par with originals, IT Act / Rule 9A); MeitY statement that issued DigiLocker documents are deemed at par with originals; Digital India on X, 29 Nov 2025, authentic-app warning; Moneycontrol, 30 Nov 2025, fake DigiLocker apps advisory; Times of India Education, 11 Dec 2025, student guidance to use official sources.

A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. The report says many of these orders were issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, which requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content to retain their legal protection. These are separate from blocking directions issued under Section 69A of the IT Act.

The report also says Meta has integrated its API with Sahyog to comply with the government’s 2–3-hour deadline, potentially allowing content flagged through government directions to be blocked automatically without a separate human review.

Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

You know what's normal? Corruption and mismanagement. So many countries around the world are led by governments, frequently authoritarian, which have persistently mismanaged their economies. 

Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Turkey, India etc. are all performing far below their potential because of policy failures connected to corruption and elite politics.

Notwithstanding its own corruption and mismanagement, Iran was actually outperforming many of these countries in delivering economic welfare until 2012. Ordinary Iranians were getting consistently richer until the sanctions really tightened that year.

What makes Iran unique *is* the sanctions. It is their pervasive and extreme impact that distinguishes Iran from other "normally mismanaged" countries. Unlike every other country experiencing economic malaise around the world, neither the Iranian state nor the private sector can engage in routine commerce. Iran cannot freely export its oil and non-oil goods and it even struggles to efficiently import food. The country faces a persistent and wholly artificial balance of payments crisis because of expansive U.S. sanctions pushed by your employer.

Who's to blame for this situation? You want to blame Iran's leaders for this predicament. In your view, it's their fault that they have undertaken policies that led them to be sanctioned by Trump. Assigning blame solely on one side is obviously ahistorical and reductive, but for the sake of argument let's say its correct and that only Iran should be blamed for the imposition of the sanctions. Does that actually absolve the U.S. from responsibility for the pain faced by ordinary Iranians? Absolutely not, because they U.S. is not just causing the hardship, it is also denying ordinary Iranians the means to alleviate the economic pain they are enduring.

Once again, we can look to other countries for a guide. When an economic crisis hits Pakistan or Argentina or South Africa, ordinary people take matters into their own hands. When things get really extreme, one form of recourse is emigration. Those who do emigrate send remittances back to their countries to support their suffering family members. Ordinary Iranians cannot do this. They are uniquely encumbered by U.S. sanctions and related policies.

If they can get a visa, Iranians can scarcely afford to emigrate to most countries and are banned from the U.S. altogether by racist policies. Those who are abroad cannot easily send money back to Iran because U.S. sanctions policy makes banks and money service businesses cower from processing payments to Iranian bank accounts.

So in effect, the sanctions have created a crisis, trapped ordinary Iranians in the crisis, and denied them the means to shield themselves from the pain of the crisis. Even if you refuse to believe that "maximum pressure" sanctions are an abnormal and amoral tool or that the U.S. government should be held responsible for their imposition, you cannot skirt the fact that sanctions deny Iranians the basic means to protect themselves from the fallout of sanctions ostensibly intended to target elites. People are getting poorer, hungrier, more desperate in a country that until quite recently had a large and growing middle class.

These conditions arose because the goal of sanctions stopped being "behavior change" years ago. The goal is to turn Iran into a weak and dysfunctional state, even if that means crushing the livelihoods and aspirations of 90 million people.

The Trump administration keeps speaking of the Islamic Republic as a "sinking ship." If ordinary people were a priority, they'd at least be thrown a lifeline. But in Iran, as in Cuba, Afghanistan, and Venezuela, people are being left to drown and people like you, who hold the rope in their hands, stand there blaming the Iranian regime for your own lack of moral action.

Is it too hard to simply call on the Islamic Republic to behave as a normal state, or does honest analysis now require laundering regime responsibility through the vocabulary of "blockade" and "starvation"? This framing is either intellectually lazy or purposefully crafted to mislead, and it abandons the first duty of serious analysis: locating causation where the evidence puts it.

Every government's baseline responsibility is to pursue foreign and economic policies that serve its people's prosperity. Tehran has done the opposite for three decades and the record predates U.S. secondary sanctions by a wide margin. 

The Majles Research Center itself documented in 1999 that 63.5% of privatizations between 1989 and 1998 went to foundations and parastatals, not a real private sector, not to the ordinary Iranians. Khamenei's Article 44 decree transferring the commanding heights to IRGC-linked and bonyad entities was issued in May 2005, five years before CISADA was passed in the U.S. Congress. IRGC economic control was estimated at ~60% by 2009.

text:
South Korea blocks Polymarket over illegal gambling concerns

South Korea has ordered domestic access to Polymarket to be blocked after determining that the platform facilitates gambling activities prohibited under the country’s laws.

The Korea Communications Standards Commission made the decision following a review launched in July at the request of the National Police Agency and the National Gambling Control Commission.

One of the most significant parts of the decision is how regulators interpreted Polymarket’s structure.

The platform argued that it operates through smart contracts on a peer-to-peer, non-custodial basis and therefore should not be treated like a traditional gambling operator.

Regulators rejected that argument.

Authorities pointed to Polymarket’s role in setting market rules, facilitating crypto deposits and withdrawals, and collecting fees from certain activities. From South Korea’s perspective, using blockchain infrastructure does not change the underlying nature of the product.

The decision also expands Polymarket’s international regulatory challenge.

South Korea joins more than 30 jurisdictions that have restricted or blocked the prediction market platform, including France, Spain, Germany and Australia.

The broader issue extends beyond Polymarket: being peer-to-peer and non-custodial may reduce control over user funds, but it does not necessarily remove regulatory responsibility for the product being offered.

text:
THE DRUG ROUTE INTO INDIA

A fact based investigation from Afghanistan and Pakistan to Punjab, from Myanmar to the Northeast, and from the border to India's streets

The Indian drug problem is often presented as a story about addicts.

That is the wrong place to begin.

The real story begins thousands of kilometres away, in places where opium is cultivated, synthetic drugs are manufactured, armed groups control territory, criminal organisations operate across borders and legitimate trade can be used to conceal illegal cargo.

By the time a packet of heroin reaches a young person in Punjab, or a tablet of methamphetamine reaches a college student in Kerala, the product may already have passed through several countries, several intermediaries, shell businesses, transport networks, financiers and local distributors.

India sits between two of the world's most important illicit drug producing regions.

To the west lies the Golden Crescent, centred historically on Afghanistan and extending through Pakistan and Iran.

To the east lies the Golden Triangle, centred on Myanmar, Laos and Thailand.

India shares a 3,323 kilometre border with Pakistan and a 1,643 kilometre border with Myanmar. It is therefore not simply a destination market. It can also become a transit country. 

And the nature of the threat is changing.

The old image of the Indian drug trade was largely heroin and opium. The newer picture contains methamphetamine, MDMA, LSD, cocaine, synthetic stimulants, pharmaceutical drugs and drugs ordered through encrypted communications and delivered through increasingly sophisticated logistics.

The most important question, therefore, is not whether India has a drug problem.

It does.

The question is what happens when two international drug corridors meet an enormous domestic market.

That is where this story begins.

---

CHAPTER ONE

THE GOLDEN CRESCENT

Afghanistan, Pakistan and the western route into India

For decades Afghanistan has been one of the world's principal sources of illicit opium.

The geography explains part of it. The politics explains another part. Decades of conflict weakened state control over remote areas, while opium provided farmers, traders and armed groups with a highly profitable commodity that could move across borders.

But there is an important fact that is sometimes missed in today's discussion.

Afghanistan's opium economy has changed dramatically since the Taliban announced its ban on poppy cultivation.

UNODC estimates that Afghanistan cultivated approximately 232,000 hectares of opium poppy in 2022. By 2025 that had fallen to approximately 10,200 hectares. Estimated opium production fell to 296 tonnes in 2025, down 32 percent from 2024 and dramatically below the pre ban period. UNODC estimated that the 2025 crop could produce approximately 22 to 34 tonnes of export quality heroin. 

That does not mean the Afghan drug threat disappeared.

Existing stocks remain.

Trafficking networks remain.

Processing and distribution networks remain.

And the trade has increasingly adapted.

The western drug corridor now has several important components.

Afghanistan remains a source of opiates.

Pakistan provides a major geographical corridor between Afghanistan and India.

Iran provides another major trafficking corridor and maritime route.

The Arabian Sea provides access to India's western coast.

The product can then move inland.

This is why the Indian authorities increasingly describe the western drug problem not simply as smuggling, but as an organised transnational network.

UNODC has noted that heroin traditionally entered South Asia through the India Pakistan land border, but that the pattern has changed. Iran became an important departure point for shipments identified by Indian authorities, with a substantial proportion entering India by sea. 

The western route therefore has multiple doors.

The land border is one.

In 2025, an NIA case involving drone delivered explosives and arms resulted in convictions of nine accused. The investigation linked the operation to Pakistan based and Germany based terrorist handlers and the Khalistan Zindabad Force. 

That is why the term narco terrorism has entered India's security vocabulary.

It does not mean every drug smuggler is a terrorist.

It means that where criminal drug networks intersect with terrorist financing, weapons trafficking or terror organisations, the drug trade becomes a national security problem.

---

# CHAPTER FOUR

## THE INDIAN SIDE OF THE NETWORK

The international supplier is only one part of the machine.

Someone has to receive the consignment.

Someone has to store it.

Someone has to transport it.

Someone has to distribute it.

Someone has to collect the money.

Someone has to launder the proceeds.

And someone has to protect the network from detection.

This is where the Indian drug trade becomes more complicated.

The evidence from major investigations points to a layered structure rather than a single organisation.

At the top can be an overseas supplier or handler.

Below that can be an Indian receiver.

Then come transporters and warehouse operators.

Below them are local distributors.

At the bottom are street dealers and users.

The money moves in the opposite direction.

The drugs move down.

The money moves up.

The system can involve legitimate businesses, rented premises, bank accounts, properties and apparently ordinary commercial transactions.

The Mundra investigation exposed the use of shell import companies. The Attari investigation exposed the use of legitimate trade documentation, godowns, Indian entities, bank accounts, property purchases and hawala. 

There is another layer.

Officials themselves can sometimes become compromised.

In April 2025, Punjab Police arrested eight people in a Pakistan backed drug cartel investigation, including a DRI inspector, according to police. The investigation also identified Dubai based hawala operators. 

In another Punjab case in 2025, police arrested a head constable along with three employees of Punjab State Power Corporation Limited in a heroin trafficking investigation. 

These cases do not prove that government agencies as institutions are part of the drug trade.

They prove something more uncomfortable.

A large criminal economy can sometimes penetrate institutions designed to stop it.

That is the difference between corruption being an isolated crime and corruption becoming an enabling component of organised crime.

---

# CHAPTER FIVE

## POLITICS ENTERS THE PICTURE

This is the chapter where facts must be separated from political claims.

There is evidence of individual politicians and political workers becoming accused or arrested in drug related investigations.

There is not evidence sufficient to say that an entire political party is a drug trafficking organisation.

Those are completely different claims.

Punjab provides several examples.

Former Congress MLA Satkar Kaur, who later joined the BJP, was arrested by Punjab Police in October 2024 in a case involving alleged heroin supply. Police said 100 grams of heroin was recovered during a decoy operation. 

In 2025, Shiromani Akali Dal leader and former Punjab minister Bikram Singh Majithia was arrested in a disproportionate assets investigation arising from a drug case. Punjab Vigilance Bureau alleged that more than Rs 540 crore in drug money had been traced in the investigation. The allegations remain matters for the legal process and should not be treated as a conviction merely because an arrest occurred. 

In 2026, an AAP backed village sarpanch in Tarn Taran was arrested by NCB after investigators reported the seizure of 18 kilograms of heroin. 

[3 /n]

text:
Another AAP local leader was arrested in Amritsar in 2026 in a case involving 4.3 kilograms of heroin and weapons, according to police reports. 

The pattern is more useful than the party labels.

Different political affiliations have appeared in different cases.

That tells us that the drug economy is not automatically loyal to one ideology.

It is loyal to money.

The same principle applies to the police.

Individual police officers have been arrested in drug cases.

That does not mean Punjab Police is part of the drug trade.

It means any system handling enormous quantities of illegal money is vulnerable to infiltration.

The correct response is therefore not to declare an entire political party, police force or government agency guilty.

The correct response is to follow the money, the communications, the properties, the bank accounts and the chain of custody until the evidence identifies the individuals involved.

That is precisely why financial investigations have become increasingly important.

---

# CHAPTER SIX

## THE SECOND FRONT

### Myanmar and the Golden Triangle

Now move east.

The geography changes.

The problem does not.

Myanmar sits at the centre of the Golden Triangle, historically one of the world's major opium producing regions.

But the Golden Triangle has undergone a major transformation.

Methamphetamine has become increasingly important.

UNODC describes the Golden Triangle as a major hub for both opium and synthetic drug production and says methamphetamine has become the dominant drug in seizure data in the region. Methamphetamine seizures in East and Southeast Asia increased substantially over the past decade. 

The heart of the problem is Shan State.

Remote terrain.

Weak governance.

Long running armed conflict.

Cross border trade.

Criminal networks.

Armed groups.

And enormous profits.

These conditions create an environment in which drug manufacturing and trafficking can survive even when governments conduct enforcement operations.

UNODC has reported that criminal organisations and armed groups in the Golden Triangle sometimes cooperate around illicit economies and that political instability and corruption in Myanmar, particularly in Shan State, have aggravated the problem. 

The important point is that this is not a simple story of one organisation manufacturing drugs.

It is an ecosystem.

Manufacturing networks.

Armed groups.

Traffickers.

Financial operators.

Transporters.

Corrupt intermediaries.

And international criminal organisations.

The exact participants can change.

The business model remains.

---

# CHAPTER SEVEN

## THE DRUGS COMING FROM MYANMAR

The principal concern for India's Northeast is heroin and methamphetamine.

Methamphetamine appears in different forms.

Yaba tablets are methamphetamine based tablets widely trafficked in the region.

Crystal methamphetamine is another form.

The Northeast is especially exposed because India shares a 1,643 kilometre border with Myanmar through Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram. 

The problem is not theoretical.

UNODC has documented the westward movement of methamphetamine from Myanmar into South Asia.

Its 2025 regional synthetic drugs report noted that methamphetamine trafficking flows from Myanmar into northeastern Indian states continued in early 2025. The report also cited a Mizoram seizure of 236.44 kilograms of methamphetamine tablets in May 2025 and a seizure of 30.4 kilograms of methamphetamine tablets in Assam in April 2025. 

Myanmar's own production remains substantial.

UNODC estimated Myanmar's potential opium production at 995 tonnes in 2024. 

But the bigger strategic concern is the synthetic market.

Synthetic drugs do not depend on agricultural land in the same way as opium.

A laboratory can produce enormous quantities.

Production can move.

Precursors can move.

How a Full Government Audit of Schools & Colleges Actually Works (India)
In India, a complete end‑to‑end audit of schools and colleges is not one single “inspection”; it’s a layered system with financial, compliance, performance and social audits done by different bodies at different levels.

Below is the practical, step‑by‑step picture of how this is supposed to work on the ground.

1. Who Actually Audits Education Institutions?
For Government Schools & Colleges
Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) – through its field offices (Accountant General, Audit).
Does performance audits and compliance audits of state education departments, schemes (Samagra Shiksha, PM POSHAN/midday meal, scholarships, infrastructure, etc.).
Example: CAG has audited “quality of school education” and “outcomes of higher education” in states like Punjab and Odisha, covering enrolment, infrastructure, teacher posts, fund utilisation, etc. https://t.co/qhcGNJZN7e

State Education Departments (Directorate of School Education, Higher Education, etc.)
Internal checks, inspections by Block Education Officers (BEOs), District Education Officers (DEOs/BSAs), and directorates.
These are more operational: teacher attendance, infrastructure, midday meal, records, etc.

Social Audit Units (under state governments, guided by central rules)
Since 2026, the Ministry of Education has formally empowered Gram Sabhas to conduct social audits of schools under Samagra Shiksha and PM POSHAN.
A small team (usually 4–5 members: 3 from Social Audit Unit + 2 local representatives) visits schools, checks registers, documents, facilities, and then presents findings in a Gram Sabha meeting. Issues can only go to higher‑level “jan sunwai” after Gram Sabha approval. livehindustan

For Private / Aided Schools & Colleges

Statutory audits under Companies Act / Societies Registration Act / Trust laws (financial statements, tax compliance).

Regulatory inspections by:
State governments (for affiliation, recognition, fee regulation).
UGC / AICTE / NCTE / Bar Council / Medical Council, etc., depending on the type of institution.
NAAC / NBA for accreditation (quality audit, not just financial).

Recent example: Telangana ordered inspections of private universities on 9 key parameters; non‑compliance can lead to stoppage of admissions, exam forms, results, etc. news18

2. What Exactly Gets Audited? (End‑to‑End Scope)

A “complete audit” typically covers four layers:

A. Financial Audit
All grants and funds: state plan funds, central schemes (Samagra Shiksha, RUSA, PM POSHAN, scholarships, hostels, etc.).

Expenditure: salaries, infrastructure, teaching–learning material, midday meal, transport, maintenance.

Procurement: tenders, vendor payments, stock registers.

Done by:
CAG (for government institutions and schemes).
Chartered Accountants (for private/aided institutions as statutory audit).

B. Compliance / Regulatory Audit

Are institutions following:
RTE Act norms (for schools): teacher–pupil ratio, infrastructure standards, no‑detention (as applicable), fee norms, etc.
UGC / AICTE / other council regulations: faculty qualifications, student intake vs approved seats, infrastructure, labs, libraries, fees, scholarships, exam processes.
Affiliation board rules (CBSE, state boards, universities).

CAG and state inspection teams routinely check this as part of performance audits. https://t.co/MWTQBWVBzq
C. Performance / Outcome Audit

This is where CAG and some state audits go beyond “money spent” to “what actually happened”:
Typical parameters:

Access: enrolment rates, dropout rates at primary/upper primary/secondary/higher secondary.

Infrastructure: classrooms, toilets (separate for girls), drinking water, electricity, boundary wall, ramps for disabled students, libraries, labs, computer rooms.

Teachers: sanctioned vs actual posts, vacancies, attendance, qualifications, training.

Learning outcomes: test scores, pass percentages, transition rates (often via sample testing or board results).

Schemes implementation: midday meal quality and regularity, textbook distribution, scholarship disbursement, transport, hostels.

Monitoring: whether district/block officials actually inspected schools, acted on complaints, maintained records.
CAG’s Odisha school audit, for example, explicitly looked at whether “universal access” was achieved, quality ensured, and monitoring effective, and found many schools still lacking prescribed infrastructure. uniindia

D. Social Audit (Community‑Level Check)

Under the new 2026 guidelines:

Who: Gram Sabha + Social Audit Unit team.

What they check:
School registers (enrolment, attendance, midday meal, funds).
Infrastructure: toilets, water, electricity, boundary wall, classrooms, safety, ramps.
Implementation of schemes: PM POSHAN, scholarships, textbooks, transport.
Direct feedback from children and parents.

3. Step‑by‑Step: How a Full Audit Is Conducted (Typical Flow)

Step 1: Planning & Selection

CAG or state audit department selects:
Which districts/blocks,
Which schemes (e.g., Samagra Shiksha, PM POSHAN, higher‑education grants),
Time period (e.g., 2018–19 to 2022–23). uniindia

For social audits, the state Social Audit Society plans a calendar (e.g., “X schools in Y districts in Z days”). livehindustan

Step 2: Data Collection

Audit teams collect:

Records from Secretariat, Directorate, District and Block offices.

School/college files: admission registers, attendance, staff records, fund utilisation, procurement files, midday meal records, scholarship lists, exam records.

Questionnaires / proformas filled by school heads and officials. https://t.co/qhcGNJZN7e
Step 3: Field Inspection / Test Checks

Joint inspection of a sample of institutions (e.g., 70 out of 111 schools in some CAG audits). https://t.co/qhcGNJZN7e

Physical verification:
Toilets, water, electricity, boundary wall, classrooms, labs, libraries, ramps.
Teacher presence, student strength, midday meal being served.

Interviews with:
Headmasters/principals, teachers, students, parents, SMC members.

In citizen‑led drives (like the CJP school audit), volunteers are asked to:

Visit schools,

Check 10 categories (water, toilets, electricity, teacher strength, textbooks, scholarships, midday meal, safety, transport, records, accessibility),

Record video evidence and send forms to the organizing group. newsreel

Step 4: Analysis & Findings

Audit teams:

Compare actual situation vs norms / rules / budget allocations.

Identify gaps:
Missing infrastructure,
Vacant teacher posts,
Irregularities in funds, midday meal, scholarships,
Poor learning outcomes, high dropouts.

Classify issues by:
Level (school, block, district, state),
Type (financial irregularity, compliance breach, performance failure).
Step 5: Draft Report & Exit Meeting
Audit team prepares draft findings.

Holds an exit meeting with concerned officials (e.g., BEO, BSA, district education officer, college principal).

Issues a notice / P2HP (Preliminary Two‑Headed Paragraph) summarising key observations. scribd

Step 6: Institutional Response

The head of the institution (e.g., Headmaster / Principal) must submit a written response within a fixed time (often ~4 days in some state audit manuals). scribd

Departments may also submit explanations and corrective action plans.
Step 7: Final Audit Report

CAG or state audit office incorporates responses and issues a final audit report.

Reports are tabled in:
State Legislature (for state education audits),
Parliament (for all‑India or major scheme audits).

These reports are public and often become the basis for media stories and parliamentary questions. https://t.co/qhcGNJZN7e

Step 8: Follow‑Up & Accountability
Government departments are expected to:
Submit Action Taken Reports (ATRs) on audit recommendations.
Fix infrastructure, fill vacancies, recover misused funds, tighten processes.

In practice, follow‑up is often weak; many audit findings remain unaddressed for years, which is exactly the frustration you’re expressing.

4. Where Does “Complete E2E Audit” Break Down in Reality?

Systemically, the process exists, but problems are:

Sampling, not 100% coverage: CAG and state audits usually test‑check a subset of schools/colleges, not every single one every year.

Fragmented responsibility:
Multiple departments (school education, higher education, finance, social welfare for scholarships, women & child for some schemes).
Multiple regulators for higher education (UGC, AICTE, councils, state governments).

Weak enforcement:
Audit reports highlight issues, but no automatic penalty unless political/executive will exists.
Citizen and social audits expose problems, but escalation depends on Gram Sabha pressure and media/NGO follow‑up. livehindustan

Private institutions:
Inspections happen, but often after complaints or court cases; systematic, periodic, public performance audits of every private college/university are not uniformly done across India. news18

5. If You Want a “Real” Complete Audit, What Should Happen?

A truly end‑to‑end, no‑escape audit system would look like:

Mandatory annual social audit for every government school by Gram Sabha, with:
Standard checklist (infrastructure, teachers, funds, schemes).
Publicly uploaded reports (district dashboard).
Periodic CAG‑style performance audits covering:
All districts in a rolling 3–5 year cycle.
Both schools and colleges, government and aided.

Regulatory audit for every private college/university:
Fixed parameters (faculty, infrastructure, fees, admissions, exams, placements).
Public rating; automatic sanctions (no admissions, no exam forms) for non‑compliance, as Telangana is attempting. news18

Single public portal:
For each institution: audit reports, ATRs, infrastructure status, teacher vacancies, fund utilisation.

Clear accountability chain:
School level → BEO → BSA/District Officer → State Director → Minister.
For each failure, the responsible officer is named in the report and tracked until resolved.

This is essentially what the rules already allow; the gap is in consistent execution and enforcement, not in the absence of a process.

A woman was riding pillion to work, about 3 km from her own house, on a road she must have used hundreds of times.

The scooter braked, skidded on a slush covered damaged stretch, and threw her into the path of a goods vehicle.

Her name was Medha Akarsh.

She was 32, from Kerala, and worked with the Employees Provident Fund Organisation in Bengaluru. She leaves behind her husband and a 3 year old son.

This week she was travelling on Ananth Nagar Main Road, near Electronics City Phase 2, riding pillion with a colleague. A pedestrian moved towards the middle of the road. The car in front braked suddenly. The rider braked, and the scooter went out from under them on the broken surface.

She was taken to a private hospital and died there.

That evening more than 400 residents came out onto the streets of Ananth Nagar holding candles and phone torches.

They were not there about the driver. They were there about the road.

A case is registered at the Electronic City traffic police station and police are looking for the driver of the goods vehicle. The Karnataka Labour Minister, Santosh Lad, said there was a possibility a pothole contributed, and also said the presence of a pothole did not mean the government had neglected infrastructure.

Now the numbers, because they are on record.

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways told the Lok Sabha that potholes killed 9,438 people in India between 2020 and 2024. In 2020 the figure was 1,555. By 2024 it had risen to 2,385. It is going up, not down.

Karnataka reported more than 2,700 grievous injuries from potholed roads in that period.

In 2018 the Supreme Court called the pothole death toll unacceptable and noted it was higher than the number killed in terror attacks. It said victims should be entitled to compensation.

In 2022 the Karnataka High Court said in open court that it felt guilty every time it read about someone dying on a Bengaluru road.

None of it worked. A woman still died on a slush covered road this week, 3 km from her house.

Here are 3 things worth knowing, because they are the difference between a statistic and a case.

First, these deaths are undercounted. Bengaluru Traffic Police have said their pothole death data only includes cases where the first information report explicitly states the road condition caused it. If the FIR does not say it, the death is never counted as a pothole death. One officer told a newspaper that their own people have a soft corner for civic officials, because everyone is part of the same system.

So if this happens to a family you know, the FIR must record the condition of the road. In writing. That single line decides whether the death exists in the data at all.

Second, the conviction rate for these cases is poor. Deaths get reported. Almost nobody is held responsible.

Third, and this is the part most people do not know. In October 2025 the Bombay High Court imposed strict liability on civic bodies for pothole deaths. It fixed compensation at 6 lakh rupees for a death caused by poor road conditions and up to 2.5 lakh rupees for injuries. Strict liability means the family does not have to prove negligence. The condition of the road is enough.

That judgment is from another High Court, so it does not bind Karnataka. But it exists, it is on the record, and it can be cited.

The roads are not an act of god. They are built by contractors, signed off by officials, and paid for with our money.

Somebody approved that stretch of road. Somebody was paid for it.

The Knights of Columbus (KOC) is a global Catholic fraternal service order founded by Blessed Michael J. McGivney. Membership is limited to practicing Catholic men. It is led by Patrick E. Kelly, the order's 14th Supreme Knight.

The organization was founded on March 29, 1882, as a mutual benefit society for working-class and immigrant Catholics in the United States. In addition to providing an insurance system for its members, it has grown to support refugee relief, Catholic education, local parishes and dioceses, and global Catholic social causes. The Knights of Columbus have played an active role in politics ever since its formation, and promote the Catholic view on public policy issues around the world.

The organization also provides certain financial services to the individual and institutional Catholic market. Its wholly owned insurance company, a Fortune 1000 company based on its annual revenue, underwrites more than two million insurance contracts, totaling more than $123 billion of life insurance in force as of 2025. The order also owns the Knights of Columbus Asset Advisors, a money management firm which invests in accordance with Catholic social teachings.

As of 2025, the Knights reported having over 2.2 million members around the world. Women may participate in KOC through the Columbiettes and other female auxiliaries, and boys may join the Columbian Squires. The Order comprises four different "degrees", each one of which exemplifies one of the core principles of the order. There are more than 17,000 local Knights of Columbus councils around the world, including over 400 on college campuses.

Organization and principles
The order is dedicated to the principles of charity, unity, fraternity, and patriotism.[44] Membership is restricted to men, at least 18 years of age, who are practicing Catholics in union with the Holy See and are in good standing with the Church.[45] As of October 2025, there were over 2.2 million Knights of Columbus worldwide, with the majority in North America.[46][47][48][49][50]

After his induction and completion of the Exemplification of Charity, a new member becomes a First Degree Knight. He then progresses through the Second and Third Degrees after completing the subsequent Exemplifications of Unity and Fraternity. A Third Degree Knight is considered to have attained full "Knighthood" status. Privileges of Third Degree membership include the ability to serve as a local council officer, and admission to state and Supreme Council business meetings.

A Third Degree Knight in good standing is eligible to complete the Exemplification of Patriotism and progress to the Fourth Degree. This is an optional degree, but represents the highest ideals of the order. A Knight who has attained this level is addressed as "Sir Knight".

Each member belongs to one of more than 17,000 local councils around the world.[47][51] Most are based in Catholic parishes, though some have their own council hall within a community. Each local council works to assist with the needs of its community consistent with the principles of the order.

The college councils program, started at Catholic University of America in 1898, was created to promote the moral, intellectual and spiritual development of college men on campuses throughout the world.[65] The oldest continuously running college council is the University of Notre Dame Council #1477, chartered in 1910.[66] Councils at seminaries ("seminarian councils") are classified as college councils. As of 2026, there are more than 37,000 knights at 320 college councils worldwide.[52]

Throughout most of its history, the Knights of Columbus has provided active support to members of the armed forces and their families. As of 2024, there are more than 50 military councils in military bases throughout North America and around the world.

A Knight who has attained the Fourth Degree also belongs to a Fourth Degree assembly. Fourth Degree Knights are men who have chosen to embrace the order's fourth principle of patriotism. Fourth Degree assemblies get their members from multiple councils within a local geographical area. They lead the efforts to reach out to veterans and active military and to embody the fact that one can be a faithful Catholic and also be a faithful citizen.[67] As of 2024, there are more than 3,600 Fourth Degree assemblies worldwide. The 125th anniversary of the Fourth Degree was celebrated in February 2025, presided over by Cardinal Timothy Dolan.[68]

Fourth Degree assemblies may form Color Corps, an elective division of the Fourth Degree, whose distinctive presence in parades, wreath-laying ceremonies, Confirmations and other Catholic functions are a visible reminder of the Knights' service to their communities. Fourth Degree Color Corps are often the most visible arm of the Knights.[69][70]

The Supreme Council is the governing body of the order. It elects insurance members to serve three-year terms on a 24-member Board of Directors.[71][72] Leaders' salaries are set by the board of directors and ratified by the delegates to the Supreme Convention.[73] The seven-figure salaries of senior KOC officers have been criticized as excessive.[73][74]

In 1969, the Knights opened a 23-story headquarters building in New Haven.[75][76]

Michael Joseph McGivney (August 12, 1852 – August 14, 1890) was an American Catholic priest based in New Haven, Connecticut. He founded the Knights of Columbus at a local parish to serve as a mutual aid and insurance organization, particularly for immigrants and their families. It developed through the 20th century as the world's largest Catholic fraternal organization.

The cause for his canonization started in the Archdiocese of Hartford in 1996; in March 2008, Pope Benedict XVI declared McGivney "Venerable" in recognition of his "heroic virtue".[1] On May 27, 2020, Pope Francis announced that McGivney had been approved for beatification, which officially occurred on October 31, 2020.[2]

Early life
Childhood and youth
Michael McGivney was born in Waterbury, Connecticut, on August 12, 1852, to Irish immigrant parents, Patrick and Mary (née Devine) McGivney. He was the eldest of 13 children, six of whom died in infancy or childhood. Patrick worked as a molder at a brass mill in Waterbury.

McGivney attended public school in Waterbury. Termed a well behaved and proficient student, he was able to graduate high school in 1865 at age 13. McGivney then started working in one of brass mills in Waterbury, making metal spoons.[3][4] While still a teenager, he decided that he wanted to become a priest.

Studies for the priesthood
In 1868, at age 16, McGivney entered the Séminaire de Saint-Hyacinthe in Saint-Hyacinthe, Quebec, in Canada. He continued his studies in 1871 at Our Lady of Angels Seminary in Lewiston, New York.[3]While at Our Lady, he and other seminarians formed a baseball team; McGivney was described as a "naturally talented ballplayer."[5]

A year later, in 1872, McGivney enrolled in the Collège Sainte-Marie de Montréal, operated by the Jesuits in Montreal, Quebec. Patrick McGivney died in 1873, forcing his son to leave Sainte-Marie.[6]At this point, he could not afford more seminary training. However, seeing McGivney's potential, Bishop Francis Patrick McFarland of the Diocese of Hartford elected to pay for the seminarian's remaining education at St. Mary's Seminary, in Baltimore, Maryland.

Establishing Knights of Columbus
During the second half of the 19th century, the Catholic hierarchy in the United States became concerned about Irish Catholic men joining extremist secret societies such as the Molly Maguires or the Fenian Brotherhood.[10]The bishops were very receptive to the creation of fraternal groups that embrace Catholic values and American patriotism. From his own experience, McGivney recognized the devastating effect on immigrant families of the father's untimely death. Many of these families were split, with the children suffering the loss of parents and estrangement from the Catholic Church.[6]

Blue laws (also known as Sunday laws, Sunday trade laws, and Sunday closing laws) are laws restricting or banning certain activities on specified days, usually Sundays in the western world. The laws were adopted originally for religious reasons, specifically to promote the observance of the Christian day of worship. Since then, they have come to serve secular purposes as well.

Blue laws commonly ban certain business and recreational activities on Sundays, and impose restrictions on the retail sale of hard goods and consumables, particularly alcoholic beverages.[1][2] The laws also place limitations on a range of other endeavors—including travel, fashions, hunting, professional sports, stage performances, movie showings, and gambling.[3][4] While less prevalent today, blue laws continue to be enforced in parts of the United States and Canada as well as in European countries, such as Austria, Germany, Norway, and Poland, where most stores are required to close on Sundays.[3][5][6][7][8]

In the United States, the Supreme Court has upheld blue laws as constitutional despite their religious origins if supported by secular justifications. This has resulted in the provision of a day of rest for the general population.[9][10] Meanwhile, various state courts have struck down the laws as either unenforceable or in violation of their states' constitutions. In response, state legislators have re-enacted certain Sunday laws to satisfy the rulings while allowing some of the other statutes to remain on the books with no intention to enforce them.[11][failed verification]

text:
⚖️ SUPREME COURT BACKS “ALTERNATE REMEDY FIRST” RULE IN GST MATTERS! 🏛️📢

Yesterday, by order dated 18.08.2026, the Supreme Court supported the view that where an efficacious statutory remedy is available under the relevant law, the same should ordinarily be exhausted instead of invoking writ jurisdiction, unless a case falling within the recognised exceptions is demonstrated. ⚖️📜

🔹 The Delhi High Court had declined to entertain a writ challenging a GST SCN and consequential order, despite pleas of lack of jurisdiction, mechanical/pre-determined proceedings and violation of natural justice, holding that these grounds could be examined in appeal under Section 107 of the CGST Act.

🔹 The Supreme Court found “no error not to speak of any error of law” in the High Court's approach and granted 4 weeks to file the statutory appeal. Importantly, all legal contentions—including alleged deficiencies in the SCN—were left open before the Appellate Authority. 🧑‍⚖️📑

⚖️ Takeaway: Availability of an effective statutory appeal remains a strong restraint on exercise of extraordinary writ jurisdiction—mere pleading of jurisdictional or natural justice grounds may not, by itself, persuade the Court to bypass the appellate mechanism. 🏛️

MarginMart Infosystems Pvt. Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner CGST, Delhi North, SLP(C) No. 26494/2026, order dated 18.08.2026 (SC), arising from W.P.(C) 9013/2026, order dated 09.07.2026 (Delhi HC).

@Outkick

AN OPEN LETTER TO THE WNBA
Ambiguity invites absurdity.
Last week yours produced two grown men declaring for the WNBA draft. One of them is six-foot-ten.
I have spent close to forty years reading documents other people wrote. Contracts, statutes, plea agreements, ordinances nobody has opened since Nixon. The most dangerous sentence in any of them is not the one that says something wrong. It is the one that sounds finished and isn't.
I will confess something before I say a word about yours. I have left language soft on purpose. Most lawyers have. You leave a word loose because pinning it down means having the fight today, in the room, with people who are tired and want to go home. So you let it ride. You tell yourself everybody in here knows what that means. Then years later somebody who was never in that room reads it cold, and it turns out nobody knew, and it is not your call anymore.
You have a new collective bargaining agreement this season. The eligibility section says only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA.
Now look for the definition.
There isn't one. No test, no standard, no sentence anywhere saying what the word means. Reporters went looking this month for a policy explaining how transgender or intersex eligibility actually gets decided in your league. They could not find one, and when they asked you, nobody answered.
The value, though, you have broadcast for a decade. On August 1 one of your coaches told reporters that every kid has a right to sports, and she has worn the shirts and written the op-eds to match. Your players union released a statement embracing justice, equity, diversity and inclusion. Nobody has to guess where you stand. You have told us at volume for years.
So two former NBA players read your rulebook, took your stated value at its word, and applied it to themselves.
Your commissioner sent teams a memo calling the matter complex and nuanced, said fair competition remains a high priority, and handed it to a task force of team presidents and general managers meeting this week. Your union said its players will not be used as political pawns.
Watch what did not happen there.
Nobody answered with the rule. There was no rule to answer with.
You cannot enforce a definition you were too afraid to write.
What came back instead was an argument about motive. You are saying these men do not really mean it, and maybe they don't. But a standard that only holds when the institution approves of your reasons is not a standard. It is a mood.
Let me be fair to you, because you have a point that deserves saying out loud instead of shouted past.
No player born male has ever played in your league as an openly transgender woman. Not one, ever. Anybody selling a five-alarm fire at the professional level is selling something. And that same coach said something in the same breath that almost nobody quoted, which is that this question needs real nuance once you get past puberty into elite competition, and that reasonable people ought to be able to find common ground.
She is right about puberty, and that concession is the entire argument, which is worth sitting with for a second because she is the one who made it and nobody made her.
Male puberty builds a longer skeleton, a bigger heart and lungs, denser bone, more fast-twitch fiber, a wider hand. No announcement reverses any of it. Women's sports exist as a separate category for that reason and no other.
What a grown adult does privately with their own body is between them, their doctor and their God. It is a different question entirely from who lines up across from a nineteen-year-old with a scholarship on the line.
If you raised a daughter, coached one, or sat in the bleachers while one learned what it meant to compete, you already know the difference.
And let me be unfair to my own side.
Those two men did not fix anything last week. They made content. One of them lasted three games in the NBA more than a decade ago. The other had an eleven-year NBA career. They will both get a week of bookings, a spike in downloads and a merch cycle out of this, and then they will move on, because that is the business they are in now. The problem does not move on. It stays exactly where it was, on somebody else's desk, and that somebody does not have a podcast.
A stunt is not a standard. It only proves one is missing.
Tennis has already been through all of this, and it is worth two minutes of your time.
In 2013 Serena Williams said men's and women's tennis were almost two different sports, and that Andy Murray would beat her 6-0, 6-0. The room laughed with her. Four years later John McEnroe said essentially the same thing and was a misogynist by lunch.
But the woman who matters most to this argument is not Serena Williams.
It is Martina Navratilova, who has spent seven years saying it and taking the beating for it. Martina and I have tangled before, and we agree on very little. She endorsed Kamala Harris. She has never had a kind word for this president. She came out in the 1980s when it cost something real. Her old coach, Renée Richards, was one of the first professional athletes in this country to transition publicly, and she coached Martina to two Wimbledon titles. She still says women's sports are not a place for failed male athletes.
When somebody I argue with that often lands where I land, I listen harder, not less.
Billie Jean King, who built the same house with her, disagrees. King has signed the briefs and given the interviews and says inclusion is the point.
Two women. Same generation, same fight, same trophy case. They cannot agree.
That is precisely why you write it down. When the two people who built the category land in opposite places, that is not a reason to stay quiet. That is a siren telling you somebody has to decide and put a name on it.
And here is what makes your silence so strange. Nearly everybody else already found the nerve to pick a side.
Twenty-seven states passed laws. The NCAA rewrote its policy and limited women's competition to athletes assigned female at birth. The United States Olympic and Paralympic Committee, a separate body from the IOC, did the same. The WTA adopted an eligibility policy built around screening for the SRY gene, ordinarily by saliva, cheek swab or blood, and is catching real fire for it from doctors who call the test too blunt and privacy advocates who have a point.
They do not all use the same rule. They do not even all agree on the science. But at least you can find the rule.
And on June 30 the Supreme Court held that Title IX permits schools to limit girls' and women's teams to biological females, and that the Idaho and West Virginia laws do not violate equal protection. Justice Kavanaugh framed the question as whether schools may determine eligibility for women's and girls' sports based on biological sex, and answered that they may.
Read that last word carefully. May.
The Court did not order anybody to do anything. It handed the decision back to the institutions and told them it is theirs to make. Which means you have now been handed this question twice, once by the country and once by the Court, and your answer both times has been a meeting.
Every one of those bodies took incoming for deciding. That is what happens when you write something down. A written rule has an author. It can be argued with, appealed, amended, repealed. Somebody stands behind it in daylight and eats the criticism.
A blank page cannot be appealed. It can only be walked through.
Now here is the part almost nobody talks about, and it is the question nobody asks.
Where are the laws protecting the boys?
Go read those state statutes instead of the headlines about them. In Florida, in West Virginia and in others, the legislature answered both halves in the same breath. Girls may play on boys' teams. Boys may not play on girls' teams.
One paragraph. Two directions. Only one of them needed a rule.
The Court did it too. There is a footnote in that opinion saying nothing in it should be read to limit biological females competing on male or co-ed teams.
Nobody marched about that half. No task force was convened to protect the boys. Nobody built a movement to keep the girls out.
And sure, it happens. A girl makes varsity as a placekicker and it is national news for a week. A girl keeps goal on the boys' side and holds her own. Good for her, seriously. But notice where it happens, which is the handful of spots where the physical gap matters least, and notice that when it does happen nobody files anything. Nobody has ever needed to.
Everybody already knows why. That is the thing nobody will say into a microphone, and it is the only reason any of this is treated as difficult.
So decide. If self-identification is your standard, then those two men qualify and you should stand up and say so out loud. If biology is your standard, publish it and defend it like everybody else has had to.
You do not get to hold both and pick between them based on who is asking.
And understand what is actually on the table while you deliberate.
You spent twenty-nine years being told this would not last. Now attendance is up thirty-four percent to over three million. Your national viewership is the best it has been since 1998, and you outdrew the NHL. Your All-Star game pulled 3.2 million this July, up forty-four percent in a year. And you are one season into an eleven-year media deal that grew from two point two billion dollars to three point one.
You are still arguing with your own players about whether any of it counts as profit yet. Which means every bit of that is a bet on people who just showed up and have not committed to anything yet.
That is the moment you have chosen to be undecided in, with the ink barely dry on the deal.
You finally got America to look. This is a hell of a time to blink.
Keep stalling and this stops being a policy question. It becomes a bit. Every former player with a phone and a grievance gets a free week of attention at your expense, and your players spend their season answering questions about it instead of playing. You will be a circus, and not the good kind, and not one of the women who built this will have done anything to earn that.
I have watched a lot of your games this season. Your officials have not been shy. Quick whistle, quick technical, and the message is always the same. Somebody has to make the call, and it will not be the crowd.
Take your own advice. Because if you will not make this call, it gets made anyway, just not by you.
None of us out here are wearing stripes. We do not need to be. There is no review on the call the crowd makes. No appeal, and nobody at the table to hear your side.
It just shows up as an empty seat.
Which brings me to the people whose opinion on this outranks yours and mine both.
The women.
If you are a woman reading this, this part belongs to you.
You built this. Equal prize money at the Open did not fall out of the sky in 1973, somebody stood in a room and demanded it. And nobody handed this league those three million seats. Women filled them. That was work, generations of it, and it is worth one written sentence.
Men should not compete in women's sports.
Not in the WNBA. Not on a college roster. Not in a Pasco County gym on a Friday night, floor wax and a buzzer and somebody's grandmother three rows up in a folding chair she brought from home.
But here is what actually keeps me up, and it is true whether you agree with that last line or not.
I am not really writing to a league. You have lawyers, a commissioner, a communications department and a task force. You will survive this either way, and you know it.
The person who cannot is an athletic director in some small district, in an office that smells like copier toner, with a schedule magnet on the filing cabinet from a printing company that went under years ago. A mother sits down across from him and asks a simple question about who her fifteen-year-old is competing against on Friday. He has no task force. No general counsel down the hall, nobody drafting a memo. He has a binder with nothing in the relevant tab, and he has to answer her before the bus leaves Thursday.
Your ambiguity becomes his responsibility.
A league can convene committees until the leaves turn. That man cannot.
So whether you agree with me or think I am dead wrong, do me one favor this week.
Find out what rule your granddaughter is actually playing under.
Pull up your own school district's policy. Not the mission statement. Not the values page. The actual policy. Find the sentence.
Then see whether there is a second one.
Ambiguity invites absurdity. Kevin Hayslett

Safe harbour provision allows platforms to maintain status and not be responsible for user generated content ‘as long as it abides by lawful directives given by the govt, Sanjay Hegde tells RT India.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s statement on wrongful content takedown by social media platforms 

Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s statement on the Delhi Police notice directing X to remove content from the platform.

According to media reports, the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (“IFSO”) unit of the Delhi Police Special Cell has issued several notices to X, citing the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (“IT Rules 2021”), following complaints filed with the Delhi Police alleging circulation of “derogatory, malicious and defamatory content” targeting constitutional heads, particularly the Prime Minister, on the social media platform. The IFSO has also registered an F.I.R. under Sections 351(3), 353(2) and 356(2) of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita 2023, against several social media handles for posting such content.

In its “Intimation to Intermediary for Disabling Access to Unlawful Information” notices issued to X,  purportedly under provisions of IT Rules 2021, the IFSO directed the platform to:

- Delete/remove the alleged post/video from the platform immediately.

- Provide the complete registrant details including full name, address, contact details and email ID, of the X account ID holder who posted such content, as well as the login and logout details of the said account, along with corresponding time and date stamp, or any other details relevant for investigation.

 - To preserve information/ records relating to the said posts for future investigation, and furnish a certificate u/s  63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in respect thereof.

This is not the first instance of large-scale removal of posts, as even earlier on 27 July 2026, Delhi Police reportedly instructed multiple social media intermediaries to take down posts/videos uploaded during the Jantar Mantar Protests that allegedly contained offensive or abusive remarks against the Prime Minister. Moreover, the Delhi Police’s social media monitoring team has been specifically engaged in monitoring online platforms for such content, and upon identifying objectionable posts, notices are issued to the concerned intermediaries directing them to remove the identified content.

At the outset, the legislative scheme of the IT Act 2000, does not contemplate/ permit the authorisation of the Delhi Police to direct the takedown of online content from social media platforms.

The power to block public access to online information or content is exclusively traceable to Section 69A of the IT Act 2000, which vests such power solely in the Central Government, or an officer specially authorised by it.  Whereas, Section 79(3)(b) of IT Act merely grants safe harbour to intermediaries, subject to compliance with due diligence obligations. In no circumstance can Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000 or IT Rules 2021 confer a power upon the Central or State Government to devise a mechanism or appoint any agency/ officer for regulating or restricting free speech online. Reliance is placed on Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (para 121).

Notably, the IT (Blocking) Rules 2009 already outline procedure and rules for the designation of an officer, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, empowered to issue directions under Section 69A for blocking public access to online information. However, neither Section 69A nor the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009 authorise the Central Government, or any State executive, to constitute a Nodal Agency empowered to direct the blocking of public access to online content.

Despite the above legislative scheme, on 26 December 2024, the Lieutenant Governor of the NCT of Delhi, purportedly in exercise of powers under the first proviso to Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT  Rules 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000, issued a Notification appointing the Delhi Police as the Nodal Agency and Deputy Commissioners of Police (of various divisions) as designated officers for issuing takedown notices. Consequently, the Delhi Police has been issuing takedown notices pursuant to the said Notification.  However, this Notification, being founded upon a provision and subordinate legislation that do not authorise the creation of such a mechanism, is ex facie illegal and ultra vires the IT Act 2000. The legality of the said Notification has been challenged by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in a Petition before the Delhi High Court on the aforesaid ground, among others. The Petition is registered as W.P.(C) 7650/2025, titled “Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors.”

Without prejudice to the aforesaid, both Section 69A and Section 79(3)(b) read with IT Rules 2021, outline overbroad grounds. While Section 69A empowers the Central Government to issue notice for blocking public access to online information on overbroad grounds such as "public order"; Section 79(3)(b) read with the IT Rules 2021 outline expansive grounds such as content’s use in the commission of an unlawful act relating to public order, decency or morality, defamation, etc., or where such information is prohibited under any prevailing law.  Since these grounds are decided by an executive order, without any judicial determination, their overbroad nature renders them susceptible to misuse and overreach. Therefore, even mere profanity, satire, or genuine criticism may be directed to be removed pursuant to such orders. This leaves the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression vulnerable.

The risk of misuse and overreach is further exacerbated by the compliance regime applicable to intermediaries. An intermediary is likely to err on the side of over-compliance rather than independently assess the legality of a removal request, owing to the extremely limited timeline for compliance and the severe consequences of non-compliance. Under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021, an intermediary is required to comply with a removal order within three hours, leaving virtually no scope for any meaningful independent assessment to guard against misuse or excessive application of such powers. Further, failure to comply exposes the intermediary to the risk of imprisonment for up to 7 years and fine for requests issued u.s. 69 A [Section 69A(3)], or the loss of safe harbour protection for orders issued u.s. 79(3)(b) [Section 79].

Moreover, when mere profanity expressed in anger against a governmental policy, or as part of political criticism, becomes the subject of penal investigation, it seriously undermines the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. We condemn any penal action in such circumstances, as it creates a significant chilling effect on the exercise of free speech by citizens, who are entitled to express their disagreement, dissatisfaction, or anger towards governmental policies through peaceful expression and dialogue.

Our team can help individuals understand their options and navigate the available redress mechanisms.
